name: Hydrogen
property: Atomic number 1 — the lightest and most abundant element in the universe.
description: I make up about 75% of all the mass in the universe, and combined with oxygen I form water.

name: Helium
property: Atomic number 2 — a noble gas that barely reacts with anything.
description: I'm used to fill party balloons and airships, and breathing me makes voices sound squeaky.

name: Lithium
property: Atomic number 3 — the lightest metal on the periodic table.
description: I'm used in the rechargeable batteries that power phones, laptops and electric cars.

name: Beryllium
property: Atomic number 4 — a lightweight, brittle, toxic metal.
description: I'm used in aerospace components and in the windows of X-ray machines because I let X-rays pass through easily.

name: Boron
property: Atomic number 5 — a metalloid essential for plant growth.
description: I'm found in borax and boric acid, and I'm added to glass to make it resistant to heat, as in Pyrex.

name: Carbon
property: Atomic number 6 — found in every living thing on Earth.
description: In one form I'm soft graphite; in another I'm diamond, the hardest natural material.

name: Nitrogen
property: Atomic number 7 — makes up about 78% of the air you breathe.
description: Farmers use compounds of me as fertiliser to help plants grow, even though I'm mostly unreactive as a gas.

name: Oxygen
property: Atomic number 8 — makes up about 21% of the air around you.
description: You need to breathe me to survive, and plants release me during photosynthesis.

name: Fluorine
property: Atomic number 9 — the most reactive element on the periodic table.
description: I'm added to toothpaste and drinking water to help protect teeth from decay.

name: Neon
property: Atomic number 10 — a noble gas that glows reddish-orange.
description: I light up the glowing signs outside shops and bars.

name: Sodium
property: Atomic number 11 — a soft metal that reacts violently with water.
description: Combine me with chlorine and I become table salt.

name: Magnesium
property: Atomic number 12 — burns with a brilliant white light.
description: I'm essential for the chlorophyll that makes plants green, and I'm used in lightweight alloys for cars and planes.

name: Aluminium
property: Atomic number 13 — the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust.
description: I'm lightweight, resist rust, and get made into drink cans and kitchen foil.

name: Silicon
property: Atomic number 14 — the key ingredient in computer chips.
description: Ordinary sand is mostly made of my dioxide.

name: Phosphorus
property: Atomic number 15 — glows faintly in the dark in one of its forms.
description: I'm essential in DNA, and I'm found in match heads and fertilisers.

name: Sulfur
property: Atomic number 16 — a bright yellow solid at room temperature.
description: Combined with hydrogen, I smell like rotten eggs, and volcanoes often release my compounds.

name: Chlorine
property: Atomic number 17 — a toxic, yellow-green gas.
description: I'm used to disinfect swimming pools and drinking water.

name: Argon
property: Atomic number 18 — the most abundant noble gas in Earth's atmosphere.
description: I'm used to fill light bulbs because I don't react with the hot filament inside.

name: Potassium
property: Atomic number 19 — reacts even more violently with water than sodium.
description: Bananas are famous for containing me, and my symbol comes from the Latin 'kalium'.

name: Calcium
property: Atomic number 20 — makes up most of your bones and teeth.
description: I'm found in milk and other dairy products, and limestone is made of my compounds.

name: Scandium
property: Atomic number 21 — a soft, silvery transition metal.
description: I'm added to aluminium alloys used in baseball bats and aerospace parts because I make them stronger without adding much weight.

name: Titanium
property: Atomic number 22 — as strong as steel but much lighter.
description: I'm used in aircraft, spacecraft, and some hip replacements.

name: Vanadium
property: Atomic number 23 — a hard, silvery-grey transition metal.
description: I'm added to steel to make it stronger and more resistant to impact, which is why I'm used in tools and construction beams.

name: Chromium
property: Atomic number 24 — gives stainless steel its shine and rust resistance.
description: I'm electroplated onto metal to give bathroom taps and car bumpers a shiny finish.

name: Manganese
property: Atomic number 25 — essential in steelmaking to remove impurities.
description: I'm a key ingredient in dry-cell batteries and in strengthening steel.

name: Iron
property: Atomic number 26 — the main metal used to make steel.
description: I carry oxygen around your body as part of haemoglobin in red blood cells.

name: Cobalt
property: Atomic number 27 — used to give glass and ceramics a deep blue colour.
description: I'm a key ingredient in the rechargeable batteries used in phones and electric cars.

name: Nickel
property: Atomic number 28 — a hard, silvery-white metal resistant to corrosion.
description: Despite my name, coins that share it barely contain me anymore in most countries.

name: Copper
property: Atomic number 29 — conducts electricity extremely well.
description: I turn green over time — think of the Statue of Liberty.

name: Zinc
property: Atomic number 30 — coated onto steel to stop it rusting.
description: Mixed with copper, I make the alloy brass, and I'm also found in sunscreen.

name: Gallium
property: Atomic number 31 — melts in the palm of your hand at just under 30°C.
description: I'm a party-trick metal that turns to liquid at close to room temperature, and I'm used in LEDs and semiconductors.

name: Germanium
property: Atomic number 32 — a brittle, grey-white metalloid.
description: I'm used in fibre-optic cables and infrared optics because I let infrared light pass through easily.

name: Arsenic
property: Atomic number 33 — a notoriously toxic metalloid.
description: Historically used as a poison, I'm now mainly used in semiconductors and some pesticides.

name: Selenium
property: Atomic number 34 — its electrical conductivity changes with light.
description: That light-sensitive property meant I was once used in photocopiers and light meters.

name: Bromine
property: Atomic number 35 — one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
description: I'm a reddish-brown, sharp-smelling liquid used in some flame retardants.

name: Krypton
property: Atomic number 36 — a noble gas named after the Greek word for 'hidden'.
description: I'm used in some energy-efficient fluorescent lights and in high-speed photography flash lamps.

name: Rubidium
property: Atomic number 37 — a soft, silvery metal that ignites spontaneously in air.
description: I'm used in precision atomic clocks and in some fireworks to give a purplish-red colour.

name: Strontium
property: Atomic number 38 — gives fireworks their brilliant red colour.
description: My compounds are also used in some toothpastes made for sensitive teeth.

name: Yttrium
property: Atomic number 39 — a silvery transition metal often grouped with the rare earths.
description: I'm used to make the red colour in older television screens and in some LED lights.

name: Zirconium
property: Atomic number 40 — highly resistant to corrosion, even from acids.
description: My oxide, cubic zirconia, is used as a cheaper diamond substitute in jewellery.

name: Niobium
property: Atomic number 41 — used in superconducting magnets.
description: I'm used in MRI machines and particle accelerators because of my superconducting properties at very low temperatures.

name: Molybdenum
property: Atomic number 42 — has one of the highest melting points of any element.
description: I'm added to steel to make it stronger at high temperatures, which is useful in aircraft parts and drill bits.

name: Technetium
property: Atomic number 43 — the lightest element with no stable isotopes.
description: I don't occur naturally on Earth in any real quantity — I'm produced artificially and used in medical imaging.

name: Ruthenium
property: Atomic number 44 — a rare, hard, silvery-white metal.
description: I'm alloyed with platinum and palladium to make them harder for use in electrical contacts and jewellery.

name: Rhodium
property: Atomic number 45 — one of the rarest and most expensive precious metals.
description: I'm used to coat catalytic converters in cars to reduce harmful exhaust emissions.

name: Palladium
property: Atomic number 46 — can absorb hydrogen gas up to 900 times its own volume.
description: I'm a key metal used in catalytic converters to clean up car exhaust fumes.

name: Silver
property: Atomic number 47 — the best electrical conductor of any element.
description: I'm used in jewellery, cutlery and coins, and my symbol comes from the Latin 'argentum'.

name: Cadmium
property: Atomic number 48 — a soft, toxic, bluish-white metal.
description: I was once widely used in rechargeable nickel-cadmium batteries, though I'm now heavily restricted due to my toxicity.

name: Indium
property: Atomic number 49 — a soft, silvery metal that makes a high-pitched 'cry' when bent.
description: I'm used in the transparent conductive coatings on touchscreens and flat-panel displays.

name: Tin
property: Atomic number 50 — used to coat steel cans to stop them rusting.
description: Mixed with copper, I make the alloy bronze.

name: Antimony
property: Atomic number 51 — a brittle, silvery metalloid.
description: I'm used in flame retardants, and ancient Egyptians used my compounds as eye makeup.

name: Tellurium
property: Atomic number 52 — one of the rarest stable elements in the Earth's crust.
description: I'm used in solar panels and in alloys to improve the machinability of steel and copper.

name: Iodine
property: Atomic number 53 — turns from solid straight to a purple vapour when heated.
description: I'm added to table salt to help prevent thyroid problems.

name: Xenon
property: Atomic number 54 — a heavy, colourless, mostly unreactive noble gas.
description: I'm used in some high-intensity headlights and in the ion engines that power some spacecraft.

name: Caesium
property: Atomic number 55 — the most reactive metal on the periodic table.
description: I'm used to define the second — atomic clocks use my vibrations to keep incredibly precise time.

name: Barium
property: Atomic number 56 — a soft, silvery-white alkaline earth metal.
description: Doctors use a compound of me as a 'barium meal' to make the digestive system show up clearly on X-rays.

name: Lanthanum
property: Atomic number 57 — the first of the lanthanide 'rare earth' elements.
description: I'm used in camera and telescope lenses because I improve their optical clarity.

name: Cerium
property: Atomic number 58 — the most abundant of the rare earth elements.
description: I'm used in self-cleaning ovens and in the flints of cigarette lighters.

name: Praseodymium
property: Atomic number 59 — a soft, silvery rare earth metal.
description: I'm used to colour glass and ceramics yellow, and in magnets used in some electric motors.

name: Neodymium
property: Atomic number 60 — used to make the strongest permanent magnets known.
description: My magnets are found inside headphones, hard drives and wind turbine generators.

name: Promethium
property: Atomic number 61 — the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes.
description: I'm radioactive and extremely rare in nature, but I've been used in luminous paint and small nuclear batteries.

name: Samarium
property: Atomic number 62 — forms powerful magnets when combined with cobalt.
description: Samarium-cobalt magnets keep their strength at very high temperatures, useful in headphones and motors.

name: Europium
property: Atomic number 63 — the most reactive of the rare earth elements.
description: I produce the red and blue phosphors used in old TV screens and in euro banknotes to help prevent forgery under UV light.

name: Gadolinium
property: Atomic number 64 — strongly attracted to magnetic fields at room temperature.
description: I'm injected as a contrast agent to make MRI scans clearer.

name: Terbium
property: Atomic number 65 — a silvery rare earth metal.
description: I produce the green light used in some energy-efficient fluorescent lamps and in older TV screens.

name: Dysprosium
property: Atomic number 66 — has one of the highest magnetic strengths of any element.
description: I'm added to neodymium magnets to help them keep working at high temperatures, such as in electric car motors.

name: Holmium
property: Atomic number 67 — has the highest magnetic strength of any naturally occurring element.
description: I'm used in some medical and industrial lasers, including surgical lasers.

name: Erbium
property: Atomic number 68 — a rare earth metal used in fibre-optic technology.
description: I'm added to the glass in fibre-optic cables to amplify light signals over long distances.

name: Thulium
property: Atomic number 69 — the least abundant naturally occurring rare earth element.
description: I'm used in some portable X-ray devices, since certain isotopes of me can emit X-rays without needing mains power.

name: Ytterbium
property: Atomic number 70 — used in some of the world's most precise atomic clocks.
description: I'm one of the elements being explored to build even more accurate atomic clocks than caesium.

name: Lutetium
property: Atomic number 71 — the hardest and densest of the lanthanide elements.
description: I'm used in some medical imaging scanners, including PET scans.

name: Hafnium
property: Atomic number 72 — highly resistant to corrosion and heat.
description: I'm used in the control rods of nuclear reactors because I absorb neutrons well.

name: Tantalum
property: Atomic number 73 — extremely resistant to corrosion, even from acids.
description: I'm used in the tiny capacitors found inside smartphones and laptops.

name: Tungsten
property: Atomic number 74 — has the highest melting point of any metal.
description: I was used as the glowing filament inside old incandescent light bulbs.

name: Rhenium
property: Atomic number 75 — one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust.
description: I'm added to superalloys used in jet engine turbine blades because I withstand extreme heat.

name: Osmium
property: Atomic number 76 — the densest naturally occurring element.
description: I'm alloyed with other metals to make extremely hard-wearing fountain pen nibs and instrument pivots.

name: Iridium
property: Atomic number 77 — one of the most corrosion-resistant metals known.
description: A thin layer of me found in rock layers worldwide is one of the key pieces of evidence for the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs.

name: Platinum
property: Atomic number 78 — a dense, silvery-white metal that barely reacts with anything.
description: I'm used in jewellery and as a catalyst in car exhaust systems.

name: Gold
property: Atomic number 79 — one of the least reactive elements there is.
description: I'm a soft, shiny yellow metal that never tarnishes, and my symbol comes from the Latin 'aurum'.

name: Mercury
property: Atomic number 80 — the only metal that's liquid at room temperature.
description: I was once used in thermometers, but I'm toxic so I've mostly been phased out.

name: Thallium
property: Atomic number 81 — a soft, toxic metal once nicknamed 'the poisoner's poison'.
description: I was once used in rat poison, but I'm now heavily restricted due to my extreme toxicity.

name: Lead
property: Atomic number 82 — a soft, dense, toxic metal.
description: I was once common in paint and petrol, but I'm now heavily restricted due to my toxicity.

name: Bismuth
property: Atomic number 83 — forms strikingly colourful, stair-stepped crystals.
description: I'm used in some stomach medicines like Pepto-Bismol, and I'm one of the least toxic heavy metals.

name: Polonium
property: Atomic number 84 — intensely radioactive, discovered by Marie Curie.
description: I was named after Poland, Marie Curie's homeland, and I'm infamous for having been used as a poison.

name: Astatine
property: Atomic number 85 — the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth.
description: I'm so radioactive and short-lived that only a few grams of me exist naturally across the whole planet at any moment.

name: Radon
property: Atomic number 86 — a radioactive noble gas that can seep into buildings from the ground.
description: I'm colourless and odourless, but I'm a leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers after long-term exposure.

name: Francium
property: Atomic number 87 — one of the rarest and most unstable naturally occurring elements.
description: I'm so radioactive and short-lived that scientists estimate less than a gram of me exists in the Earth's crust at any time.

name: Radium
property: Atomic number 88 — glows faintly in the dark due to its radioactivity.
description: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered me, and I was once used in glow-in-the-dark watch dials before the dangers of radioactivity were understood.

name: Actinium
property: Atomic number 89 — gives its name to the actinide series of elements.
description: I glow with a faint blue light in the dark because of my intense radioactivity.

name: Thorium
property: Atomic number 90 — a radioactive metal being explored as a nuclear fuel.
description: I'm being researched as a safer alternative to uranium for future nuclear power reactors.

name: Protactinium
property: Atomic number 91 — one of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements.
description: I'm extremely rare, toxic and radioactive, and I have almost no uses outside scientific research.

name: Uranium
property: Atomic number 92 — the heaviest naturally occurring element.
description: I'm used as fuel in nuclear power stations.

name: Neptunium
property: Atomic number 93 — the first transuranium element, named after the planet Neptune.
description: I was the first element made artificially that's heavier than uranium, produced in a laboratory in 1940.

name: Plutonium
property: Atomic number 94 — used as fuel in some nuclear reactors and weapons.
description: I was used in the 'Fat Man' atomic bomb, and I also power some deep-space spacecraft as a heat source.

name: Americium
property: Atomic number 95 — found in a device in most homes.
description: A tiny amount of me is used inside household smoke detectors to sense smoke particles.

name: Curium
property: Atomic number 96 — named in honour of Marie and Pierre Curie.
description: I'm intensely radioactive and have been used as a compact power source on Mars rovers.

name: Berkelium
property: Atomic number 97 — named after Berkeley, California, where it was first made.
description: I was first created in 1949 at the University of California, Berkeley, and I exist only in laboratories.

name: Californium
property: Atomic number 98 — named after the US state where it was discovered.
description: I'm used as a neutron source to help start up some nuclear reactors and to detect gold and silver ores.

name: Einsteinium
property: Atomic number 99 — named after physicist Albert Einstein.
description: I was first identified in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952.

name: Fermium
property: Atomic number 100 — named after physicist Enrico Fermi.
description: Like einsteinium, I was first discovered in the fallout from a thermonuclear bomb test in the 1950s.

name: Mendelevium
property: Atomic number 101 — named after Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table.
description: I was first made one atom at a time, and I exist only in laboratory experiments.

name: Nobelium
property: Atomic number 102 — named after Alfred Nobel, founder of the Nobel Prizes.
description: I'm a synthetic element that exists for only a short time before decaying.

name: Lawrencium
property: Atomic number 103 — the last element in the actinide series.
description: I'm named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron particle accelerator used to create many synthetic elements.

name: Rutherfordium
property: Atomic number 104 — named after physicist Ernest Rutherford.
description: I'm a synthetic superheavy element that only exists for a fraction of a second after being created in a lab.

name: Dubnium
property: Atomic number 105 — named after Dubna, Russia, home to a major nuclear research lab.
description: I'm a synthetic element made by smashing lighter nuclei together in a particle accelerator.

name: Seaborgium
property: Atomic number 106 — named after chemist Glenn Seaborg.
description: I'm one of the very few elements named after a scientist who was alive at the time of the naming.

name: Bohrium
property: Atomic number 107 — named after physicist Niels Bohr.
description: I'm a synthetic superheavy element that decays within moments of being created.

name: Hassium
property: Atomic number 108 — named after Hesse, the German state where it was discovered.
description: I was first created at the GSI research centre in Darmstadt, Germany, in 1984.

name: Meitnerium
property: Atomic number 109 — named after physicist Lise Meitner.
description: I honour one of the physicists who helped explain nuclear fission, though she was overlooked for the Nobel Prize.

name: Darmstadtium
property: Atomic number 110 — named after Darmstadt, Germany, where it was discovered.
description: I was first created in 1994 at the GSI research centre in Darmstadt.

name: Roentgenium
property: Atomic number 111 — named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays.
description: I'm a synthetic superheavy element that exists for only a fraction of a second.

name: Copernicium
property: Atomic number 112 — named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.
description: I'm predicted to behave like a gas or a volatile liquid at room temperature, unlike most metals.

name: Nihonium
property: Atomic number 113 — named after Japan (Nihon), where it was discovered.
description: I was the first new element discovered by researchers in Asia, at the RIKEN institute in Japan.

name: Flerovium
property: Atomic number 114 — named after the Flerov Laboratory in Russia.
description: I'm a synthetic superheavy element, and physicists believe elements near me might be unusually stable for their size.

name: Moscovium
property: Atomic number 115 — named after the Moscow region of Russia.
description: I was created through a joint Russian-American research collaboration and confirmed as a new element in 2016.

name: Livermorium
property: Atomic number 116 — named after the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the US.
description: I'm a synthetic superheavy element that exists for only a fraction of a second before decaying.

name: Tennessine
property: Atomic number 117 — named after the US state of Tennessee.
description: I was confirmed as a new element in 2016, discovered through research involving Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

name: Oganesson
property: Atomic number 118 — the heaviest element on the periodic table.
description: I'm named after Yuri Oganessian, a scientist who led the discovery of many superheavy elements.
